summary:
The District of Columbia stands under the United States national framework, and federal policy overrides local protections for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Entry screening carries a second exposure. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. On visa applications, listing a gender other than the sex assigned at birth has been treated as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud: the State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sports would be refused, flagging applicants with an internal marking.

Facilities access is restricted in much of the country but not in the District. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Local protection in the District is not settled. Congress attached a bathroom ban to the District of Columbia, and on 5 December 2024 Axios recorded the arrest of transgender-rights activists who protested that ban at the Capitol. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places the District on its low-risk list alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin, while stating that the District may no longer be considered the most protective jurisdiction because Congress and executive action can reach it.

Document rules are tightening in the states. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template for other states, with further bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 assessment flagged Idaho as the latest state rated "Do Not Travel" for trans people, bringing the total to four, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Care access is constrained nationally for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.
tangentialFactors:
The District's low-risk rating in the July 2026 assessment rests on its own statute and court machinery, not on immunity from federal power. The assessment's own caveat is that Congress retains authority over District legislation and that executive action can reach District residents and visitors directly, which is why the same document, screening and custody exposures that apply in the four states rated "Do Not Travel" apply inside the District.

The Kansas statute of February 2026 is treated by rights groups as a template, with further bills pending in other state legislatures, so the number of jurisdictions invalidating existing trans documents is likely to grow during a visitor's planning horizon. Foreign governments have already responded to the federal document and data rules: in April 2025 CNN reported advisories issued by several countries about trans people travelling to the United States, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.
localsOnly:
The District of Columbia has no ban on trans people using facilities congruent with their gender identity, and it sits in the group of 29 states, four territories and the District that the Movement Advancement Project records as having no such ban. That local position does not shield a resident from federal facilities restrictions under Executive Order 14168 in federally funded buildings, nor from the arrest risk illustrated when activists protested the Congressional bathroom ban at the Capitol on 5 December 2024.

Residents who are trans and who come into federal custody face the same conditions as anyone else held nationally: the Federal Bureau of Prisons conversion-therapy-style policies in force from 2026, the halt in reporting of transgender prisoner numbers from 2025, and the forced-labour, beating, solitary-confinement and sexual-abuse reports in immigration detention. Residents also lose the same services as visitors when federal care provision contracts, including the specialised LGBTQ youth services withdrawn from the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in July 2025 and the Medicaid reimbursement barriers proposed in October 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope, text and current legal status of the bathroom ban that Congress attached to the District of Columbia are not sourced in this inventory; only the fact of its attachment and the December 2024 arrests are established here. Whether the ban was enacted as District legislation, as a rider on a federal spending measure, or as a standalone congressional directive is unresolved.

No source here establishes whether the District issues its own identity documents with gender markers that differ from federal records, or how District agencies treat a visitor presenting an inconsistent passport, so that question is unresolved. The July 2026 assessment's low-risk classification for the District is a legal-landscape rating; whether it reflects any measure of enforcement outcomes, hate-crime data or reported incidents in the District is not sourced.
